title: Every Balance With Fewest Deletions
statement:
You get a string s of round brackets and lowercase letters. A string is balanced when every ( has a matching ) after it and every ) matches an earlier (. Letters are ignored for balance.

Delete the fewest brackets possible so that the string becomes balanced. Return every distinct string you can get with that minimum number of deletions, in any order. Letters are never deleted. If nothing is left, the answer is [""].

examples.why: One ) must go. Deleting the first ) gives "(())a"; deleting either of the other two gives "()()a", which is listed once.
The last ( can never be matched and one of the two ) is extra: two deletions. Both ways of choosing the ) give the same string.
Every bracket is in the wrong place, so all four go, leaving the empty string.

hints: Before searching, can you count exactly how many ( and how many ) must be deleted?
Scan left to right with a counter of open brackets. A ) with nothing open must be deleted; whatever is still open at the end is the number of ( to delete. That fixes the size of every answer.

Backtrack over the string deciding keep or delete for each bracket, never deleting more of either kind than needed and never letting the open count go negative. Collect results in a set, and skip deleting a bracket when you just kept an identical one before it.

explain.intuition:
The minimum is not a mystery you search for: one left-to-right scan tells you exactly how many ) are unmatched (a ) arriving with nothing open) and how many ( are still open at the end. Every answer deletes exactly those numbers, rmOpen and rmClose, and no fewer can work.

Knowing the budget turns the search into tight backtracking: for each bracket, try keeping it, and try deleting it only if that kind still has deletion budget left. Prune any branch where a kept ) has nothing to match. At the end, keep the string if the budget is spent and nothing is open. Several deletion sets can produce the same text, as "(x))(" shows, so results go into a set.
steps: Scan once to compute rmOpen and rmClose, the brackets that must go.
Recurse with (index, open, rmOpen, rmClose, built). Letters are always kept.
For a bracket, if its kind still has budget, branch on deleting it. Then branch on keeping it: a ( raises open; a ) is only kept when open > 0.
At the end of the string, if both budgets are 0 and open is 0, add built to the result set.
Return the set as a list.
pitfalls: Returning duplicates. Deleting different copies of the same bracket in a run produces the same string.
Returning balanced strings with more than the minimum number of deletions. Fix the budget first, or stop a level-by-level search at the first level that has any valid string.
Returning an empty list when every bracket must go. The empty string is a valid answer and must be returned as [""].

complexity.time: O(2ᵇ · n) in the worst case for b brackets, far less with the budget pruning

solutions.title: Try every subset of deletions
solutions.idea: For every subset of brackets, delete it and test the result. Keep the balanced results with the smallest subset size.

solutions.title: Level-by-level search
solutions.idea: BFS where each level deletes one more bracket. The first level that contains a balanced string is the answer level.

solutions.title: Backtracking with an exact deletion budget
solutions.idea: Count the brackets that must go, then decide keep or delete per bracket without exceeding either budget or letting the open count go negative.
solutions.time: O(2ᵇ · n) worst case, heavily pruned

followups: Return just one balanced string with the fewest deletions. Can you do it in linear time?
The string also contains square brackets that must nest correctly with the round ones. What breaks in the counting step?
